analysis.one_liner: Strengthens background-check records and federal gun prosecutions while loosening interstate gun sales and transport rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced in April 2024 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This Republican-led bill pairs two very different agendas. On one side, it pushes federal agencies to submit prohibited-purchaser records to the background-check system, funds new federal gun prosecutors and ATF trafficking task forces in high-homicide cities, and raises penalties for lying on a background-check form. On the other, it expands where licensed dealers can sell guns, lets gun owners carry locked, unloaded firearms across any state line without arrest under state transport laws, and makes it harder for VA decisions to strip a veteran's gun rights. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the highest-homicide cities would get a new federal prosecution program and trafficking task forces aimed at straw purchasing. Licensed firearms dealers would gain the right to sell at temporary locations in any state and to complete more sales across state lines. Lawful gun owners traveling between states would gain a federal shield from state and local transport laws, including attorney's fees if they prevail.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Gun dealers, gun owners, high-crime cities

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal agency to identify and submit records showing a person is barred from gun possession to the NICS background-check system, and authorizes $20 million per year through 2029 for state record-sharing grants

Creates a 'Nationwide Project Exile' program adding federal prosecutors and ATF agents in the 15 U.S. jurisdictions with the worst homicide totals and rates plus 3 tribal jurisdictions, funded at $15 million per year for three years

Orders ATF trafficking task forces in the Houston, Phoenix, Dallas, and Los Angeles field divisions with at least 12 agents each, focused on straw purchasing, and creates a DOJ task force targeting felons and fugitives who try to buy guns illegally
Raises the maximum penalty for lying on a federal background-check form from 5 years to 10 years

Gives anyone transporting an unloaded, locked firearm or ammunition a federal right to pass through any state, with arrest barred unless police have probable cause the transport was unlawful, and attorney's fees for defendants who win
Lets licensed dealers sell firearms at temporary locations in any state and broadens where licensed-to-licensed transfers may occur

analysis.who_pays: States that fail to report mental-health records to the background-check system would lose 5 to 10 percent of their Byrne JAG law-enforcement grants. People in states with stricter gun-transport rules would lose those protections, since the bill overrides state and local law. Taxpayers fund the new prosecutors, agents, and grant programs.

drawbacks.text: The interstate transport provision preempts state and local firearms laws, bars arrest without probable cause, and puts the burden on the government to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that a transport was unlawful — overriding the stricter rules some states impose

A person found mentally incompetent through VA benefits administration could not be treated as federally prohibited from buying a gun unless a judge, magistrate, or other judicial authority finds them a danger to themselves or others

States would lose 5 percent of Byrne JAG funds after 18 months, rising to 10 percent after five years, if they do not report at least 90 percent of required mental-health records to NICS or pass a statute requiring it
The mandated mass-shooting study is directed to examine violent video games and other factors; video-game causation is a contested explanation that researchers have repeatedly failed to confirm

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a package deal: its strongest public-safety provisions — record-sharing with NICS, prosecuting straw purchasers, and funding federal gun prosecutions in high-homicide cities — are paired with deregulatory provisions that loosen dealer commerce and preempt state transport laws. An honest reading is that it trades enforcement muscle for expanded commerce freedom, and a legislator would have to accept the second half to get the first. The record-sharing and prosecution pieces are the more concrete, evidence-backed parts; the video-game study is the weakest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Chuck Grassley introduced S. 4104 with Sens. Ted Cruz and Thom Tillis on April 10, 2024
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day
No further action appears in the bill's history — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill died in committee

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained much from the bill's quiet death. States with stricter gun-transport laws kept their rules, since the federal preemption never passed — but communities also got none of the new federal prosecutors, NICS record improvements, or trafficking task forces the bill proposed. The gun laws on both sides of the ledger stayed exactly as they were.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans and no Democrat cosponsored; the bill never reached a vote, so there was no roll call to measure broader support.

industries.note: The bill expands where and how dealers may sell — temporary locations in any state and broader interstate transfer authority — and shields interstate transport from state enforcement. Those gains come by loosening the state-level rules that stricter jurisdictions use to limit gun access.

Easier interstate commerce and dealer flexibility could widen the customer base, but the bill also funds ATF task forces and stiffer penalties aimed squarely at straw purchasing that feeds illegal markets.

States that do not report mental-health records to the background-check system would lose 5 to 10 percent of Byrne JAG grants, and all states lose authority over interstate firearm transport. The funding penalty pushes states toward a public-safety goal, but the preemption strips their regulatory power.

industries.industry: Federal gun enforcement (ATF and U.S. Attorneys)
industries.note: The bill authorizes tens of millions of dollars a year in new agents, prosecutors, and task forces to pursue straw purchasers and traffickers, directly supporting enforcement communities ask for.
